explanation: Retinal arterial macroaneurysm is one of the few lesions that bleeds simultaneously at several levels, so preretinal, intraretinal and subretinal hemorrhage (and sometimes vitreous hemorrhage) are all classic findings. Chronic leakage from the aneurysm produces macular edema, often cystoid, together with a circinate lipid ring, so CME is expected. Cotton-wool spots are nerve fibre layer infarcts from precapillary arteriolar occlusion and belong to hypertensive, diabetic or vasculitic retinopathy, not to the macroaneurysm itself. Because most of these patients are hypertensive, cotton-wool spots may coexist in the fundus, but they are not a feature of the lesion, so B is the exception.

Pseudoexfoliation material is deposited on the lens equator and on the zonular insertions and progressively weakens them, so phacodonesis, intraoperative zonular dehiscence, capsular bag instability and late in-the-bag IOL subluxation are the defining surgical hazards; capsular tension rings and careful hydrodissection are the usual countermeasures. Poor pupillary dilatation from deposits on the iris and a rigid pupil compound the difficulty. Corneal edema does occur postoperatively because PXF eyes have reduced endothelial reserve, and PCO can follow any phacoemulsification, but neither is the characteristic intraoperative problem that makes a PXF eye a high-risk case.

The Branch Vein Occlusion Study protocol was to wait about three months after a BRVO before treating persistent macular edema, because a substantial proportion of eyes improve spontaneously as the hemorrhage and edema settle. Grid laser was then offered only if vision was 20/40 or worse and the fluorescein angiogram showed a perfused, non-ischemic macula, so A is wrong: macular ischemia is a contraindication to macular grid laser, not an indication. Option C is wrong because angiography is deliberately deferred until intraretinal blood clears enough to interpret capillary perfusion, which typically takes longer than four weeks.
concern: Answer B reflects the classic BVOS teaching that the exam is testing. Current practice has moved on: anti-VEGF therapy (and dexamethasone implant) is first-line for BRVO macular edema and is started promptly rather than after a three-month observation period.

explanation: A child with a year of slowly progressive proptosis plus choroidal folds has an orbital mass indenting the posterior globe until proven otherwise, so cross-sectional orbital imaging is the next step; MRI with contrast and fat suppression best characterises soft tissue, defines optic nerve and intracranial extension, and avoids ionising radiation in a child. Choroidal folds are a sign of posterior globe compression or hypotony, not a diagnosis, so fluorescein angiography would merely confirm the folds without explaining them. A Hess chart records the pattern of any motility restriction but does not find the cause. Slowly progressive proptosis at this age suggests optic nerve glioma, dermoid, plexiform neurofibroma or a vascular lesion, whereas rhabdomyosarcoma usually progresses over weeks.

A pontine lesion, classically a hypertensive pontine hemorrhage, interrupts the descending sympathetic fibres travelling through the brainstem to the ciliospinal centre of Budge, so parasympathetic tone is unopposed and the pupils become bilaterally pinpoint while remaining light-reactive (best seen with a magnifier). Mydriasis instead localises to the midbrain and pretectal region, or to a third nerve, ciliary ganglion or pharmacological cause. The useful topographic rule is pons equals small pupils, midbrain equals large or mid-dilated poorly reactive pupils.

No currently available anti-toxoplasma drug eradicates the encysted bradyzoites. Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, clindamycin, atovaquone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole all act on the actively dividing tachyzoites only, which is exactly why recurrences arise from cysts at the border of an old pigmented scar. Classic therapy is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine with folinic acid to protect the bone marrow, and oral corticosteroid added a couple of days after the antiparasitic cover, never as monotherapy. Option B is true: although the typical picture is a single satellite focus beside an old scar, multifocal and bilateral disease is well recognised, particularly in immunocompromised and congenitally infected patients.

Selective laser trabeculoplasty delivers sub-millijoule energy in a 3-nanosecond pulse, selectively targeting pigmented trabecular cells without coagulative damage, whereas panretinal photocoagulation delivers on the order of tens of millijoules per burn over 20 to 100 milliseconds to produce a visible retinal burn, so the total energy per application in SLT is far lower. Option C is clearly wrong: the aiming beam is placed directly on the pigmented trabecular meshwork, not posterior to it. Option A overstates the case; SLT works in both phakic and pseudophakic eyes and any difference in response between them is modest and disputed, certainly not a marked superiority in phakic eyes.
concern: Strictly, SLT has a very high peak power because its energy is delivered in nanoseconds; the statement is only true if power is read loosely as energy delivered per application, which is how the exam intends it. B is still the only defensible option since A and C are both wrong as written.

explanation: Corneal blood staining follows a large or prolonged hyphema, and the two permissive factors are raised intraocular pressure and a compromised endothelium, which together allow hemoglobin breakdown products and hemosiderin to enter the stroma, so A is true. Clearance is slow, taking months to years, and it proceeds from the limbus centripetally, so the central cornea is the last area to clear; the statement that it resolves from the centre first is therefore the false one. This peripheral-to-central pattern is what makes deprivation amblyopia a genuine risk in a young child and is one of the arguments for early surgical evacuation of a hyphema once staining begins.

Usher syndrome is defined by retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural deafness and is the commonest cause of combined deaf-blindness. Alstrom syndrome pairs a cone-rod dystrophy with sensorineural hearing loss, obesity, insulin resistance and dilated cardiomyopathy. Cockayne syndrome combines a pigmentary retinopathy with sensorineural deafness, cachectic dwarfism, photosensitivity and premature ageing. Refsum disease is defined by a cardinal tetrad of retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised CSF protein without pleocytosis, caused by phytanic acid accumulation and treated by dietary restriction of phytanic acid and plasma exchange, so on the cardinal-feature reading it is the odd one out.
concern: This question is imperfect. Sensorineural deafness and anosmia are well recognised additional features of Refsum disease and are listed as such in standard tables of syndromic RP, so strictly all four options can be associated with hearing loss. C is the defensible answer only because deafness is not part of Refsum's cardinal tetrad, whereas it is a defining feature of the other three.

explanation: Nausea, vomiting, hypotension and bradycardia after an orbital block is the picture of either central spread of anesthetic or systemic local anesthetic toxicity. Injection into the optic nerve sheath allows subarachnoid spread to the brainstem, producing confusion, contralateral amaurosis, dysphagia, apnea and cardiovascular depression, which is why resuscitation equipment must be available for every retrobulbar block. Inadvertent intravascular injection gives the same cardiodepressant picture with seizures, and anaphylaxis to hyaluronidase gives hypotension with gastrointestinal upset. Excess epinephrine is the pharmacological opposite: beta-1 mediated tachycardia with hypertension, arrhythmia, tremor and anxiety, so it is the one option that cannot generate bradycardia with hypotension.
concern: The source answers A on the strength of a passage describing brainstem anesthesia as causing hypertension and tachycardia. An early sympathetic surge is indeed described, but the classic and better documented endpoint of brainstem anesthesia is respiratory arrest with bradycardia and cardiovascular collapse, so option A can produce the stem's syndrome. Epinephrine excess cannot produce bradycardia and hypotension together, which makes C the cleaner exception. The recall is uncertain (the source itself marks option A with a question mark), so treat this as a considered second opinion rather than a correction.

explanation: Read this as a spectacle magnification question. A plus spectacle lens worn in front of a hyperopic eye magnifies the retinal image, so the corrected hyperope sees objects appearing larger, while the minus lens of a corrected myope minifies, roughly 2 percent per dioptre at standard vertex distance. That is also why an aphakic spectacle correction produces marked image magnification and why anisometropes get aniseikonia. Contact lenses largely abolish this effect because they sit at the corneal plane.
concern: The stem is badly truncated and depends on a figure that cannot be seen, so this is an interpretation rather than a certain reading. Knapp's law is the caveat: in purely axial ametropia, spectacle correction at the anterior focal point gives an image size similar to the emmetropic eye, so the magnification effect is most marked in refractive ametropia.

explanation: The established prognostic factors for uveal melanoma are tumour size (largest basal diameter and thickness), cell type (epithelioid cells carry the worst prognosis, spindle A the best), location (ciliary body involvement and anterior tumours do worse than posterior choroidal), extraocular extension, mitotic rate and increasingly the cytogenetic and gene expression profile, above all monosomy 3 and class 2 signature. Degree of pigmentation has been suggested in some series but is not an accepted independent prognostic factor and does not appear in staging or risk stratification, so it is the exception.

Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for sarcoid uveitis, given topically, by periocular or intraocular injection, or systemically, and chronic granulomatous uveitis frequently needs prolonged therapy with a slow taper, so long-term steroid is the true statement. Option B is wrong because steroid-sparing immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine, or anti-TNF agents in refractory disease) is required in a substantial proportion of patients to avoid steroid morbidity. Option A is wrong because diagnosis rests on a compatible clinical picture with tissue biopsy as the gold standard, supported by chest imaging, ACE and lysozyme; gallium scanning is only an ancillary test, useful when the panda and lambda patterns appear.
concern: The recall is incomplete and the source flags a possible missing option, so C is chosen as the best of what is presented.

explanation: Taking the stem at face value, all three listed items are recognised features of a third nerve palsy, which is why the recall is unsatisfactory. Aberrant regeneration follows compressive and traumatic palsies, and a dilated poorly reactive pupil is the hallmark of a compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Pain is the least constant feature: it is expected with an aneurysm but is variable in microvascular palsy and absent in many cases, so it is the weakest generalisation and the best answer available.
concern: The stem is truncated and probably lost a qualifier. If the original read microvascular or ischemic third nerve palsy, the answer would change: aberrant regeneration never occurs in an ischemic palsy and the pupil is characteristically spared, while pain is common. Answer with caution and treat this item as unreliable.

explanation: In adults, especially those over 50 with vasculopathic risk factors, the commonest cause of an isolated third nerve palsy is microvascular ischemia of the nerve trunk, typically pupil-sparing, painful or painless, and resolving over about three months. The vasa nervorum infarct spares the peripherally placed pupillomotor fibres, which is the anatomical basis of the pupil rule. Tumour and trauma are important but far less frequent causes, and aneurysm, although only a minority of cases, is the one that must be excluded urgently whenever the pupil is involved or the palsy is incomplete with pain.

Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is a chronic bilateral epithelial keratitis with coarse, elevated, greyish-white intraepithelial dots and a quiet conjunctiva, and it responds dramatically to low-potency topical corticosteroid; loteprednol is a good choice because its ester structure carries a lower risk of steroid-induced pressure rise during the prolonged low-dose treatment these patients need. Topical ciclosporin is a legitimate steroid-sparing alternative but is second line and slower to work. Idoxuridine and trifluridine are antivirals with no role here; idoxuridine in particular is epitheliotoxic and was historically used but is now avoided.

The classic teaching distinguishes the organisms of acute and chronic dacryocystitis: Staphylococcus aureus (with Streptococcus pyogenes and Haemophilus in children) predominates in acute suppurative disease, whereas Streptococcus pneumoniae is the organism traditionally associated with the chronic, quiet, mucocoele-type dacryocystitis behind a nasolacrimal duct obstruction. With only these two choices, A is the answer.
concern: Modern culture series are less tidy: coagulase-negative staphylococci are frequently the commonest single isolate overall, and gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas are increasingly reported in chronic cases. The pneumococcus association is a teaching convention rather than a fixed microbiological fact.

explanation: Bupivacaine is the longest acting of the four; it is highly lipid soluble and protein bound, giving roughly four to twelve hours of akinesia and analgesia, which is why it is commonly mixed with lidocaine for orbital blocks to combine rapid onset with prolonged duration. Lidocaine lasts around one to two hours, and procaine, an ester rapidly hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase, is the shortest acting. Tetracaine is a potent long-acting ester in the spinal setting but in ophthalmology it is used as a surface anesthetic with only about ten to twenty minutes of effect, so it is not a competitor for block duration. Bupivacaine is also the most cardiotoxic of the group, which matters if it enters a vessel.

Posterior subcapsular cataract sits immediately in front of the nodal point on the visual axis, so it degrades vision most when the pupil is small; near work and bright light both constrict the pupil, which is why PSC characteristically impairs near vision and causes glare and haloes more than distance acuity. Nuclear sclerosis behaves the other way round, reducing distance vision first and often improving unaided near vision through a myopic shift (second sight), so A is true. Cataract remains the leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide, so C is true, making B the false statement.

For ocular adnexal lymphoma the risk of concurrent or subsequent systemic lymphoma is strongly site-dependent, and the classic gradient runs eyelid highest, then orbit, then conjunctiva lowest, with figures commonly quoted around two thirds for eyelid, about a third for orbit and about a fifth for conjunctiva. Conjunctival lesions are typically the salmon-patch MALT type with the most indolent behaviour, whereas eyelid lesions are more often higher-grade histologies. Whatever the site, systemic workup with imaging, bone marrow examination and oncology referral is mandatory.

Benign essential blepharospasm is a focal cranial dystonia of the orbicularis oculi (often with corrugator and procerus involvement), so D is true. Like most dystonias it disappears during sleep and is aggravated by stress, bright light and fatigue, so A is true. It is treated medically, with botulinum toxin injection the mainstay and oral agents and myectomy as alternatives, so B is true. It is not commoner in men: benign essential blepharospasm has a clear female predominance of roughly two to three to one, with onset in the fifth to seventh decades, so C is the false statement.

The greatest change in refractive index in the eye occurs at the air to tear film and cornea interface, from about 1.000 to 1.376, and with an anterior corneal radius of roughly 7.8 mm this surface contributes about plus 48 dioptres, the most powerful refracting surface in the eye. The posterior corneal surface passes from cornea to aqueous, a tiny index step, and being concave to the incoming light it contributes about minus 5 to minus 6 dioptres, so the net corneal power is close to plus 43. The lens surfaces lie between aqueous and lens substance with only small index differences and together give about plus 19 dioptres in the unaccommodated eye. This is why small changes in the anterior corneal surface, whether from refractive surgery or from an unstable tear film, have such a large refractive effect.

A retrobulbar injection deposits anesthetic inside the muscle cone, so the nerves lying within the cone, namely the third and sixth nerves, are blocked first and the recti and levator are akinetic early. The trochlear nerve runs outside the muscle cone, entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure above the annulus of Zinn and travelling along the orbital roof to the superior oblique, so the superior oblique is the last muscle to be affected, and residual intorsion on attempted downgaze is the classic sign of an otherwise complete block. This is also why a truly complete akinesia may require supplementary anesthetic outside the cone.

Proparacaine (proxymetacaine) 0.5 percent is an ester topical anesthetic with onset within about 20 seconds and a duration of roughly 10 to 20 minutes, so 15 minutes is the best single figure among the options offered. Its practical advantage over tetracaine and benoxinate is that it stings far less on instillation, which is why it is preferred for tonometry, gonioscopy and paediatric examination. Duration is dose-dependent, so repeated drops for a longer procedure extend the effect, at the cost of increasing epithelial toxicity.
concern: The published range is 10 to 20 minutes, so both option B and option D can be defended; C is the mid-range figure and the safest choice.

explanation: Operating microscope phototoxicity is a photochemical injury to the RPE and outer retina and its severity is dose-dependent, that is a product of irradiance and exposure duration, so the single most effective and most practical protective measure is to keep the light exposure short and the illumination no brighter than needed. Option D is the opposite of protective: a coaxial beam focuses light directly onto the macula, so tilting the microscope off-axis reduces risk, which also makes C wrong. Option B is nonsense as written since a 200 nm filter is outside the range relevant to the visible and near-UV light involved; the useful measures are ultraviolet and short-wavelength blocking filters, oblique illumination, corneal light shields, an air bubble or opaque disc over the pupil, and lowering the light intensity.

A sixth nerve palsy produces an abduction deficit with uncrossed horizontal diplopia that is worst on gaze towards the paretic side. The patient adopts a compensatory face turn towards the side of the palsy, so that both eyes are moved into the field of gaze away from the paretic muscle's field of action, where the images fuse. A left sixth nerve palsy therefore produces a left face turn. Head tilt is the compensatory posture for a cyclovertical problem, classically the contralateral tilt of a fourth nerve palsy, not for a horizontal rectus palsy.

Equal involvement of both sexes rules out X-linked recessive inheritance, which predominantly affects males. Unaffected parents rule out autosomal dominant inheritance in a fully penetrant trait, and also exclude mitochondrial inheritance, which is transmitted from an affected mother to all her children. Two carrier parents give a one in four recurrence risk in each pregnancy with both sexes equally affected and characteristic skipping of generations, which is precisely the pedigree described, so this is autosomal recessive. Consanguinity, if present, would strengthen the inference further.

The superior oblique arises from the periosteum of the body of the sphenoid superomedial to the optic canal, close to the origin of the levator, and not lateral to the optic foramen, so B is false as written. Its functional origin, however, is the trochlea on the superomedial orbital rim, from which the reflected tendon runs backwards and laterally to insert under the superior rectus. From that functional origin the tendon makes an angle of about 51 degrees with the visual axis, which is why its primary action in the primary position is intorsion (D true) and why depression becomes its dominant action as the eye adducts (C true in the sense examiners intend).
concern: Option A is also false as transcribed: 23 degrees is the angle the vertical recti make with the visual axis, whereas the obliques act at about 51 degrees. The recall probably corrupted this figure, so the item has two false options; B is the anatomically unambiguous one and the intended answer.

explanation: A normal ESR does not exclude giant cell arteritis: a small but real proportion of biopsy-proven cases have normal inflammatory markers at presentation, which is why a compelling clinical picture (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, amaurosis fugax, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy with a chalky white swollen disc in a patient over 50) mandates high-dose steroid and temporal artery biopsy regardless of the blood results. This makes C wrong. B is wrong because ESR is a non-specific acute phase marker raised by infection, malignancy, anaemia, renal disease, pregnancy and simple ageing.
concern: Option D is arguably true as well: CRP is the more sensitive single marker and requesting both raises the overall detection rate, which is why current practice is to order ESR, CRP and platelet count together. A remains the classic and safest answer because it carries the clinically important message, but this item has two defensible true statements.

explanation: The tunica vasculosa lentis, derived from the hyaloid artery system, is the essential nutritional supply of the lens during development, before the aqueous circulation is established; it later regresses, and failure of regression leaves a Mittendorf dot, a persistent pupillary membrane or persistent fetal vasculature. Option C is clearly false because only the primary lens fibres come from the posterior epithelium of the lens vesicle; secondary fibres are laid down continuously throughout life by the equatorial epithelium at the lens bow, and are the reason no lens epithelium exists posteriorly in the adult. Options A and D quote timings that do not fit the standard sequence, in which the lens placode invaginates in the fourth week, the lens vesicle separates from surface ectoderm around day 33, primary fibres fill the vesicle in weeks five to seven, and the tunica fully invests the lens only around the third month.
concern: This item depends on a figure that cannot be seen, and the developmental dates quoted in options A and D vary slightly between textbooks, so the elimination of those options is approximate.

explanation: Bowman's layer is not a basement membrane; it is an acellular condensation of the most anterior stroma made of randomly arranged collagen fibrils, and it has no cells to regenerate it, which is why injury through it leaves permanent scarring. The true basement membrane in that region is the epithelial basement membrane, which lies on top of Bowman's layer and is secreted by the basal epithelial cells. Option C is true because collagen filaments and the interfacial matrix anchor the posterior stroma to Descemet's membrane, and D is true because the corneal endothelium, like the stroma and the anterior chamber angle structures, arises from neural crest.
concern: Option A is loosely worded: the stromal collagen that predominates is type I with type V forming heterotypic fibrils and type VI in the interfibrillar matrix, with only small amounts of type III in the normal cornea. Older texts do list types I and III together, so it is usually accepted as true, but B is the unambiguous falsehood.

explanation: For a soft lens the sagittal depth, and therefore the tightness of fit, depends on both base curve and diameter, so if the base curve is held constant and the diameter is increased, the lens vaults more and drapes more tightly on the eye. The result is a steep or tight fit with reduced movement and lag, conjunctival indentation and circumlimbal injection, the tight lens syndrome that can progress to hypoxic complications. This makes B, and the loose-fit signs of edge lift and excessive movement, all wrong. Practically, either flattening the base curve or reducing the diameter will loosen such a fit.

Polydactyly is the presence of a supernumerary digit and is a useful systemic clue in ophthalmic genetics, most notably in Bardet-Biedl syndrome, where it accompanies a rod-cone dystrophy, obesity, hypogonadism, renal disease and learning difficulty. Clinodactyly is curvature of a digit in the coronal plane, brachydactyly is abnormal shortness of the digits, and arachnodactyly is the long spidery digits of Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria, both of which are relevant to ectopia lentis but are the opposite of an extra digit.

Taking the question as the examiners intend it, the aqueous humour is the metabolic supply of the avascular anterior segment structures with which it is in direct contact, principally the lens, the corneal endothelium and the trabecular meshwork; it delivers glucose, amino acids, ascorbate and glutathione and removes metabolic waste. It also maintains intraocular pressure and hence globe shape, and is optically clear so that light passes undisturbed, so options A, C and D describe genuine functions. The examiners treat B as the exception on the grounds that the aqueous nourishes the posterior cornea rather than its epithelium.
concern: Physiologically option B is defensible and arguably true: the corneal epithelium obtains most of its glucose by diffusion from the aqueous across the stroma, while it takes oxygen from the tear film and atmosphere. Option D is also probably a garbled transcription of transparent refracting medium. This item is a poor recall and should not be relied on.

explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heterogeneous group of collagen disorders whose shared hallmarks are skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and tissue fragility with easy bruising and poor wound healing that leaves cigarette-paper scars, so A is a core feature of essentially every subtype. Option D is clearly wrong: the digits are hypermobile and often long, not short. Ocular associations to remember are blue sclerae, thin cornea and keratoconus, angioid streaks, ectopia lentis and, in the kyphoscoliotic type, globe fragility with a risk of rupture after minor trauma.
concern: Option C is also true: the kyphoscoliotic type (lysyl hydroxylase deficiency) and dermatosparaxis type are autosomal recessive, although most subtypes including the classical and hypermobile types are autosomal dominant. Kyphoscoliosis in option B is likewise real but confined to one subtype. A is the most universally true statement, but the recall probably altered the wording of the distractors.

explanation: Contact lens wear is the single largest risk factor for bacterial keratitis in the developed world, particularly extended or overnight wear, poor hygiene, topping up solutions, and exposure of lenses or cases to water; the lens creates hypoxia and epithelial compromise while acting as a biofilm-coated vector, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the characteristic organism in lens wearers. Ocular surface disease and trauma, including vegetative injury, are the other major risks. Tap water matters chiefly as the source of Acanthamoeba in lens wearers rather than as an independent bacterial risk, and systemic bacterial infection and age are not major contributors.

Alkalis raise the pH of the ocular surface and, because they saponify cell membrane lipids and penetrate rapidly through the cornea, the pH of the aqueous rises within seconds to minutes; a statement that intraocular pH falls is therefore the incorrect one. Acids by contrast coagulate stromal protein, which forms a barrier that limits deeper penetration, so an alkali injury is generally more serious than an equivalent acid injury, making C true. Immediate copious irrigation with at least a litre of saline or water, continued until the pH normalises, is the single most important intervention, and extensive epithelial loss with limbal ischemia (the whitening that predicts limbal stem cell failure) defines a severe grade with poor prognosis.

Herpetic anterior uveitis is characteristically unilateral and recurrent in the same eye, so calling bilateral disease a common presentation is the false statement; bilateral herpetic anterior uveitis should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis or suspicion of immunocompromise. The typical features are raised intraocular pressure with active inflammation, diffuse stellate keratic precipitates that are not confined to Arlt's triangle, patchy or sectoral iris atrophy with distortion of the pupil, and reduced corneal sensation from previous epithelial disease, so B and C are true. Attacks are variable in length and may run from a week to several months, needing topical steroid with antiviral cover.

The corneal epithelium and its basement membrane, along with the lens, the lacrimal gland and the eyelid epidermis, derive from surface ectoderm, not from neural crest, so C is the false statement. Neural crest cells migrate from the crests of the neural folds in the region of the forebrain and midbrain into the periocular mesenchyme in successive waves, forming the corneal endothelium first, then the corneal stroma, and then the anterior chamber angle structures including the trabecular meshwork. Neural crest also contributes the sclera, the choroidal stroma, the iris stroma, the ciliary muscle and the orbital bones and connective tissue, which is why disordered neural crest migration produces the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum such as Axenfeld-Rieger and Peters anomaly.

Prisms of the same orientation must never be stacked, because the deviation produced is greater than the arithmetic sum, so a 30 and a 40 prism dioptre base-out combination measures considerably more than 70 prism dioptres and will grossly overestimate a large deviation; large angles should be split between the two eyes or measured with a large single prism or prism bar. Perpendicular stacking of a horizontal and a vertical prism is acceptable because their effects are in different planes, so B is true. Plastic prisms are calibrated for the frontal plane position and glass prisms for the position of minimum deviation, making C true, and high plus lenses minify so the measured deviation reads less than the true angle, making D true.

The vortex veins drain the entire uveal venous circulation, that is the choroid, ciliary body and iris, and typically number four to seven, one in each oblique quadrant, exiting through the sclera behind the equator where their ampullae are visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy or scleral indentation. The retina drains separately through the central retinal vein into the superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus, so option B is the incorrect statement. Knowing the ampullae positions matters surgically, since damage during scleral buckling, strabismus surgery or drainage of suprachoroidal fluid can cause choroidal congestion or hemorrhage.

CT is superior for bone and for radiopaque or metallic foreign bodies, so orbital fracture is the classic indication, with thin-slice coronal reconstruction showing the orbital floor and medial wall and any entrapped tissue. MRI is better for soft tissue contrast, which is why it is preferred for choroidal melanoma and its extraocular extension, for posterior scleritis, and above all for the posterior fossa and any intracranial lesion, where CT is degraded by bone-hardening artefact. CT is also faster and more accessible in an emergency, and it is mandatory before MRI whenever a metallic intraocular foreign body is suspected.

The efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex runs from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus with the third nerve to the inferior division, then to the ciliary ganglion, where postganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in the short ciliary nerves to reach the iris sphincter and the ciliary muscle. The afferent limb travels in the optic nerve to the pretectal nuclei with bilateral projection through the posterior commissure, which is why the consensual response exists. The long ciliary nerves carry sympathetic fibres to the dilator and sensation from the cornea, while the lacrimal and frontal nerves are purely sensory branches of the first division of the trigeminal with no pupillary role.

Lockwood's ligament is the suspensory ligament of the globe, a hammock formed by fusion of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique sheaths with the check ligaments of the medial and lateral recti, supporting the eye from below; it is why the globe does not drop after removal of the orbital floor, and why large inferior rectus recessions can produce lower lid retraction. Whitnall's ligament is the superior transverse ligament that acts as the fulcrum redirecting the levator from a horizontal to a vertical vector. The capsulopalpebral fascia is the lower lid retractor, the analogue of the levator aponeurosis, and the lateral rectus check ligament is only one component of the suspensory system.

The retinal circulation supplies the inner two thirds of the retina, extending outwards as far as the inner nuclear layer, while the choriocapillaris supplies the outer third by diffusion, namely the outer plexiform layer, outer nuclear layer, photoreceptors and RPE. The inner nuclear layer is therefore the outermost layer served by the central retinal artery, and the outer plexiform layer is the watershed between the two circulations. This explains why a central retinal artery occlusion produces inner retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot from the intact choroidal supply at the foveola, and why paracentral acute middle maculopathy on OCT localises to the deep capillary plexus at the inner nuclear layer border.

Acute inflammation is the stereotyped innate response to any tissue injury, and chemical injury is a standard trigger alongside trauma, infection, ischemia, thermal and immunological insults, so C is true. Option A is wrong because acute inflammation is non-specific and antigen-independent, in contrast to the specific adaptive response. Option B reverses the sequence: the vascular phase of transient vasoconstriction followed by vasodilatation and increased permeability comes first, and the cellular phase of neutrophil margination, rolling, adhesion and emigration follows. Option D overstates the timescale, since acute inflammation is measured in hours to a few days and persistence beyond that marks the transition to chronic inflammation with lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages.

Accommodation begins with parasympathetic contraction of the circular fibres of the ciliary muscle, which moves the ciliary body forwards and inwards, slackening the zonules and allowing the elastic lens capsule to mould the lens into a more globular shape with steeper surfaces, a greater anteroposterior thickness and a higher refractive power. This makes D correct and directly contradicts A and B, which invoke relaxation of the circular muscle, the state that flattens the lens for distance. Option C is wrong because the anteroposterior diameter of the lens increases, not decreases, during accommodation. Pupillary miosis and convergence accompany this as the near triad but are not themselves the accommodative mechanism.

The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid just as it leaves the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve, lying within the dural sheath at that point. Once in the orbit it turns and crosses the nerve, in about four fifths of people passing over it superiorly and in the remainder beneath it, to run forwards along the medial orbital wall towards the trochlea, where it terminates as the supratrochlear and dorsal nasal arteries. Its first and clinically most important branch is the central retinal artery, which enters the nerve about 8 to 15 mm behind the globe.
concern: The artery is inferolateral at entry, so option B, lateral, is also partly correct, and if the verb turns is read as referring to its crossing then superior would be the answer instead. The recall is ambiguous, though inferior is the best single choice for its position on entering the canal.

explanation: A cilioretinal artery is a branch of the posterior ciliary circulation that emerges at the temporal disc margin with a characteristic hook and supplies part of the papillomacular bundle and macula, and the figure usually quoted in ophthalmic texts is around 20 to 25 percent of eyes, so 25 percent is the intended answer. Its clinical importance is twofold: it preserves central vision in a central retinal artery occlusion by sparing the macula, and it can itself infarct, producing an isolated cilioretinal artery occlusion, classically in association with a central retinal vein occlusion or with giant cell arteritis.
concern: Reported prevalence varies widely between series, from around 15 percent to over 30 percent depending on whether detection was clinical or angiographic, so the exact percentage is soft. Given the options, 25 percent is the closest to the commonly quoted figure.

explanation: Malignant hyperthermia, triggered in susceptible patients by volatile anesthetics and suxamethonium, presents earliest with a hypermetabolic picture: a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased minute ventilation, unexplained tachycardia, tachypnoea, masseter spasm after suxamethonium and generalised muscle rigidity. Fever is a dramatic but characteristically late sign and waiting for it delays treatment, so D is the exception. Management is to stop the trigger, hyperventilate with 100 percent oxygen, give dantrolene without delay, and treat the hyperkalaemia, acidosis, arrhythmias and myoglobinuria. This matters in paediatric ophthalmology because strabismus surgery patients have historically been over-represented in reported cases.

The optic tract runs posterolaterally from the chiasm, sweeping around the cerebral peduncle, and divides near its termination into a larger lateral root ending in the lateral geniculate nucleus and a smaller medial root carrying pupillomotor and retinotectal fibres to the pretectal nuclei and superior colliculus, so options B and C describe it correctly. Its blood supply comes chiefly from the anterior choroidal artery, with contributions from the posterior communicating artery, so A is true. A tract lesion produces an incongruous homonymous hemianopia with a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect and, in time, band or bow-tie atrophy of the contralateral disc.
concern: This item is a weak recall. The optic tract does in fact course lateral to the third ventricle along the wall of the hypothalamus, so option D is not clearly false, and option C is garbled (superior cerebral peduncle is not a standard structure). D is given as the answer only because it matches the key and no option is convincingly wrong.

explanation: The Scheie stripe (Zentmayer line) is a band of pigment deposited on the posterior lens capsule at the equator in pigment dispersion syndrome, not a trabecular finding, so C is the false statement. Sampaolesi's line is the wavy band of pigment lying on or just anterior to Schwalbe's line, seen in pseudoexfoliation and in pigment dispersion, so A is true. The scleral spur is the white band posterior to the trabecular meshwork and anterior to the ciliary body band and is the key gonioscopic landmark for grading the angle, so B is true. Schwalbe's line marks the termination of Descemet's membrane and the anterior limit of the trabecular meshwork, so D is true; an anteriorly displaced and prominent Schwalbe's line is posterior embryotoxon.

If both parents are affected by an autosomal recessive disorder, each is homozygous for the mutant allele and therefore has no normal allele to transmit, so every child must inherit two mutant alleles and every child will be affected. The probability is 1, or 100 percent. The familiar one in four figure applies to the quite different situation of two unaffected heterozygous carriers, which is not what this stem describes. The one caveat, which does not change the answer here, is genetic heterogeneity: if the two parents were affected by mutations at different loci causing a clinically similar phenotype, the children could be unaffected double heterozygotes, but for a single-gene disorder the answer is unambiguously 1.
concern: The source answers B, one in four, and its own quoted reference explicitly describes parents who both CARRY the gene, not parents who are both affected. The key has confused affected homozygotes with unaffected carriers. Two affected parents with the same recessive condition transmit it to all offspring, so the correct option is D.

explanation: During accommodation the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules relax and the elastic capsule allows the lens to become more globular, so its anteroposterior thickness increases and its equatorial diameter decreases; the anterior surface steepens most, the anterior chamber shallows slightly and refractive power rises. Saying the lens becomes thinner is therefore the exception. Convergence is correct because accommodation, convergence and miosis form the near synkinesis triad driven together, which is the basis of the AC/A ratio and of accommodative esotropia.

The lens is the most radiosensitive structure in the eye because the dividing equatorial epithelial cells are highly susceptible to radiation damage and the abnormal fibres they produce migrate posteriorly and cannot be cleared, giving the characteristic posterior subcapsular cataract; thresholds are low, in the low single-figure gray range, and the latency may be years. The cornea and retina tolerate considerably higher doses, and radiation optic neuropathy and retinopathy occur only at much higher cumulative doses, typically above 50 gray. This is why lens shielding is used during head and neck radiotherapy and why cataract is the commonest long-term ocular consequence of ocular irradiation.

Horner-Trantas dots are the discrete white chalky accumulations of degenerated eosinophils and epithelial debris that sit on the limbus in the limbal form of vernal keratoconjunctivitis, accompanied by gelatinous limbal thickening; they are transient and mark active disease. Arlt's line is the horizontal subconjunctival scar in the upper tarsus of trachoma, Fuchs spot is the pigmented macular scar of pathological myopia after choroidal neovascularisation, and Cogan's is used for a microcystic epithelial dystrophy and for a separate interstitial keratitis with vestibuloauditory disease, neither being a limbal deposit.

Stocker's line is the vertical iron line lying in the corneal epithelium just ahead of the advancing head of a pterygium, and its presence indicates that the pterygium is long-standing rather than rapidly growing. Option A is false as written because the Fleischer ring outlines the base of the cone in keratoconus, not its apex, and is best seen with a cobalt blue filter. All these lines share the same mechanism, epithelial iron deposition where the tear film pools against an abrupt change in corneal contour, which is also the mechanism of the Hudson-Stahli line of normal ageing and the Ferry line beside a filtering bleb.
concern: As transcribed, options C and D are also true statements: the Ferry line does lie in the cornea adjacent to a filtering bleb, and iron lines are well described after radial keratotomy and other keratorefractive surgery. Only A is definitely false, so the recall has probably altered the distractors; B is nonetheless correct.

explanation: Astigmatism requires a difference in refractive power between meridians of the cornea or lens. Horizontal rectus surgery, particularly resection with its tightening effect on the anterior sclera and cornea, is well documented to induce measurable corneal astigmatism, usually transient. Pellucid marginal degeneration thins the inferior peripheral cornea and produces marked irregular against-the-rule astigmatism with the classic crab-claw topography, and a subluxated lens in Marfan syndrome produces lenticular astigmatism from tilt and from the edge effect of the displaced lens. A posterior staphyloma at the macula distorts the posterior globe wall and produces high axial myopia, with retinal distortion and choroidal thinning rather than a meridional difference in refracting power, so it is the exception.
concern: A posterior staphyloma can in principle cause some irregular or oblique astigmatism through posterior segment distortion, so this is the weakest of the four rather than an absolute exclusion. It remains the best answer because the other three are all classic astigmatic causes.

explanation: Corneal-to-lens adhesion is the hallmark of Peters anomaly type II, not of aniridia, so B is the exception. Aniridia, usually from PAX6 mutation, is a panocular disorder in which the iris hypoplasia is only the most visible sign: aniridic keratopathy from limbal stem cell deficiency produces peripheral pannus and conjunctivalisation, glaucoma develops in a large proportion of patients as the rudimentary iris stump rotates over the meshwork, and foveal hypoplasia with nystagmus and optic nerve hypoplasia gives permanently reduced acuity, that is a form of visual deprivation amblyopia. Cataract and lens subluxation are also common, and sporadic cases require renal surveillance for Wilms tumour through the WAGR deletion.

The crystalline lens measures about 9 to 10 mm in equatorial diameter in the adult, while its anteroposterior thickness grows continuously throughout life because secondary fibres are laid down without any being shed, rising from about 3.5 mm at birth to around 4 mm in the fourth decade and 5 mm or more in old age. At age 40 the lens sits in the 4 to 5 mm band. This lifelong growth, with progressive nuclear compaction and loss of capsular elasticity, is the anatomical basis of presbyopia and of the age-related shallowing of the anterior chamber that predisposes to angle closure.
concern: Age 40 lies close to the boundary between options B and C, with quoted mean thickness at that age around 4.0 to 4.3 mm, so the answer depends on the source's figures; C is nonetheless the better fit.
